t: Revivalists taught that conversion was not only assent to correct doctrine but a new birth experienced in the heart, and that assurance of salvation was a normal expectation of the Christian life.
The revivals divided churches into pro-revival New Lights and anti-revival Old Lights, causing 98 schisms among New England Congregationalists, while Baptist and Methodist churches grew.
The historian Jon Butler has argued that the term Great Awakening is vague and exaggerated, because the revivals were regional and their effects minimal, while others see a larger impact.
dyk: In 1743 James Davenport ordered his followers at New London to burn wigs, cloaks, rings and other vanities, and also books by religious authors such as John Flavel and Increase Mather; he later published a retraction.
ev: Jonathan Edwards preaches on justification by faith alone, starting the Northampton revival, which spreads to 25 communities
John Wesley feels his heart strangely warmed at a Moravian meeting on Aldersgate Street
Refused pulpits in Bath and Bristol, George Whitefield begins open-air preaching at Kingswood and soon draws crowds of 10,000
Whitefield tours New England and preaches in Boston to about 15,000 and later to 30,000 people
The Presbyterian Synod of Philadelphia expels the New Side, which forms the Synod of New York
James Davenport orders the burning of wigs, cloaks, rings and books at New London
New Side Presbyterians found what becomes Princeton University
The Old Side and New Side Presbyterians reunite

f.where: Britain (England, Wales and Scotland), the thirteen North American colonies, and Pietist communities in continental Europe such as Herrnhut
f.period: revivals in the colonies from the 1710s and 1720s; Northampton revival 1734–1735; Welsh revival from 1735; Whitefield's and Wesley's open-air preaching from 1739; a great and general Awakening in New England 1740–1743; waning by 1745; revivals in the southern backcountry and slave communities in the 1750s and 1760s
f.figures: George Whitefield, itinerant preacher; John and Charles Wesley, founders of Methodism; Jonathan Edwards, Congregational minister at Northampton; Gilbert Tennent, Presbyterian New Side leader; James Davenport, controversial itinerant; Nicolaus Zinzendorf, Moravian patron; Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland in Wales; Samuel Davies, preacher to enslaved people
f.outcome: Protestant churches split into supporters and opponents of revival; Methodist and Baptist churches grew, Congregational and Presbyterian churches divided in the colonies, and a common evangelical identity emerged; historians dispute how great its effects were
